[stretchcloud]A plain text file sitting in your Downloads folder can now hijack your coding agent, and it doesn't need a single line of executable code to do it.
Forever Security caught this live on a customer machine last week. A malicious AGENTS.md planted in Downloads told Codex to install an npm package called function-color. In their broader testing, Codex followed instructions like that in more than 90% of runs. A parallel demo against Claude Code was worse in a different way: a poisoned CLAUDE.md redirected the agent's API traffic to a researcher-controlled server, exposing auth tokens the researcher then replayed against the real API. That configuration-hijack version succeeded in roughly half of Claude Code's tests.
The mechanism is almost insultingly simple. These agents treat markdown instruction files as legitimate direction the moment they're in a trusted working directory, no execution required, no malware signature to catch. Akshat Tyagi at HFS Research put the design flaw plainly: the tools conflate following an instruction with granting a privilege, and vendors have to start treating those as separate decisions.
This isn't fringe anxiety either. Omdia's latest survey found 40% of respondents only somewhat or not confident their org can secure AI agents at all, and it's the literal top trending story on this platform today. Every team running Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or any agent with filesystem access against an untrusted directory, a cloned repo, a shared drive, is exposed to some version of this.
My read: instruction files need the same review discipline as source code, not a free pass because they're markdown. Until vendors separate "read this" from "do this," Downloads folders stay a live attack surface.

[Jife790]AI has learned to process massive amounts of information, but understanding the physical world is a completely different challenge.
That’s where @vangrid_io stands out.
For Physical AI to reach its full potential, machines need more than powerful models. They need access to real world environments, spatial information, and data that reflects how things actually exist beyond a screen.
Vangrid is working at this intersection through 3D reconstruction and distributed real world data collection, helping create the foundation for AI systems to understand physical spaces in greater detail.
The bigger picture is what makes this worth watching. As machines become more integrated into everyday environments, the quality of real world data could become just as important as the intelligence of the models themselves.
We’re moving toward an era where AI won’t just analyze what we show it. It will need to understand the world it operates in.
Vangrid is building in a space that could become increasingly important as that future takes shape.

People approach artificial intelligence with different goals. Some want to explore ideas, others want to generate images, while developers need ways to integrate AI capabilities directly into their applications.
The challenge is not simply making AI more powerful. It is making that power accessible through experiences that fit different needs.
The future of AI belongs to platforms that make intelligence easier to access, easier to use, and more practical to integrate.
𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐔𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐃𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬
💡 1. For Thinkers And Researchers
AI can help people explore unfamiliar topics, organize information, brainstorm ideas, and approach complex questions from new perspectives.
🎨 2. For Creators
Image generation and other creative tools can help transform concepts into visual content, opening new possibilities for designers, storytellers, marketers, and digital artists.
💻 3. For Developers
API access can allow developers to incorporate AI capabilities into their own products, automate selected tasks, and experiment with new application designs.
⚙️ 4. For Everyday Productivity
Simple interfaces can make AI more approachable for people who want useful results without navigating complicated technical workflows.
Each pathway serves a different purpose, but the objective remains the same: helping people turn ideas into outcomes.
𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁.𝐀𝐈 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬
@B_And_AI represents an opportunity to explore AI through different models, tools, and access experiences.
The broader significance is the movement toward more flexible AI ecosystems. Rather than assuming everyone works the same way, platforms can provide different routes for people to discover and use AI capabilities.
This flexibility matters because adoption depends on more than model performance.
Users also care about accessibility, usability, response quality, available features, and the effort required to achieve their goals.
Developers may prioritize integration and documentation, while creators may care more about the quality of generated content. Everyday users may simply want a straightforward experience that saves time.
A strong AI platform must recognize these differences instead of forcing everyone into one workflow.
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐁𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐮𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐲 🚀

[altafganihar]Today we're launching @snaptrude Agent, the most advanced agent for building design.
It does real design work with you, from a site to a construction-ready LOD 400 model with structure, MEP and drawings. Then can go back to your existing software with your families intact.
About a year ago we bet the company on AI. Honestly the insight came from software engineering. It wasn't long ago that autocomplete felt like a big deal, and now engineers direct agents that write a lot of the code. I think the same shift is coming to how we design buildings, and it's already started.
Most designers I meet aren't short on skill, they're short on time. Take the call every design team dreads, the client cuts the budget by 30%. Today that's a bad month for everyone. With the agent you're the director. You decide where the cost comes out, and it updates the layout, coordinates the structure and MEP, and redoes the drawings. So when design exploration gets this cheap, we go from 3 options to 300, and more options means better buildings.
Since August our users have gone through more than 140 billion tokens, and firms like Jacobs, Studio+, Kajima, VMDO, Dekker and hundreds of others use Snaptrude today. In our early access, more than 2,000 designers have run over 25,000 tasks through the agent since September.
We also built a benchmark for this, AECBench, because in AEC an almost correct answer is still wrong. [OpenAI]Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.
Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.
To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.
To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.
In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.
As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene.

[gregisenberg]The cobra effect is one of the more interesting phenomena in startups. Once you see it, you start noticing it everywhere, in your team, your metrics and now your AI agents.
It's basically when you reward people for hitting a number, and they find a way to hit it that makes the real problem worse.
The name "Cobra Effect" comes from a story about Delhi under British rule. There were too many cobras in the city, so the government offered a reward for every dead cobra people brought in.
Instead of hunting them, people started breeding cobras so they could kill them and collect the money!
When the government found out and ended the program, the breeders let their snakes go, and Delhi ended up with more cobras than before!
I'm noticing that AI agents are making this more common. Basically, an agent will chase whatever number you give it, all day, without asking why. Tell it to make the tests pass and it might rewrite the tests. Tell it to close support tickets faster and it might close them without solving anything. It happens.
The best startups have already figured out the fix with people. Airbnb tracks bookings and host cancellations together. HubSpot takes back sales commission when a customer churns early.
The video breaks down how they did it, and it's the same playbook you'll want for your agents.

[justinsuntron]Last night, my lawyers moved to sanction World Liberty Financial @worldlibertyfi for failing to disclose, until months into my litigation against the company, that it is a citizen of the UAE 🇦🇪 . #WLFI #USD1
For those who are new to this dispute, I was one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors. In November 2024, I agreed to buy $30 million of $WLFI tokens under a Token Purchase Agreement with World Liberty, and I later increased my total investment to $45 million.
In April, I sued World Liberty, alleging that the company induced my investment through fraud and then unlawfully froze my tokens.
My Token Purchase Agreement gives me the right to bring my claims in either California federal or state court.
I chose federal court.
Federal courts can hear a case like mine only when the two sides come from different places. Foreign plaintiffs like me can sue an American defendant in federal court, but foreign plaintiffs generally cannot sue a foreign defendant there. For these purposes, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the company foreign.
In other words, so long as World Liberty and all of its owners were American, my case could be heard in federal court.
The federal court’s rules required World Liberty to file a disclosure at the start of the case identifying every one of its owners and where each is a citizen. World Liberty’s disclosure identified only one entity—World Liberty itself—and listed Florida as its sole citizenship. Its lawyers certified that they were unaware of anyone else who needed to be disclosed.
World Liberty then moved to compel arbitration, seeking to pull my case out of open court and into secret arbitration proceedings.
I opposed that motion, and my lawyers spent months and hundreds of thousands of dollars fighting it. At a hearing in August, the Court signaled that it was not persuaded that my claims belonged in arbitration. Instead, the Court ruled that certain of my claims should stay in open court, and certain claims should be sent to arbitration, and ordered the parties to meet and confer to come up with a proposed agreement on which claims stay in open court and which ones go to arbitration.
Less than a week later, World Liberty suddenly “corrected” its disclosure. Where it had previously listed only one member in its ownership chain, it now listed 22, and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE.
World Liberty now says that the federal court has no jurisdiction over my case, since its UAE citizenship means there are foreign parties on both sides of the case.
The irony is hard to miss. World Liberty’s gold paper declares that “[b]y design, World Liberty Financial is not organized offshore,” and that it is “an American, tax-paying, corporation that aims to bring DeFi to its rightful home—America.” It promises a “US-based decentralized platform” built on “American ideals of liberty, privacy, and freedom to transact,” calls private, intermediary-free transactions “a core American value,” and boasts that “[r]ather than shying away from the United States, World Liberty Financial embraces the United States as the future CRYPTO CAPITAL OF THE PLANET.”
World Liberty was proudly American 🇺🇸 when it was selling tokens. It discovered its UAE 🇦🇪 roots only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom.
World Liberty presumably always knew who its owners were. Its lawyers claim that they learned about the company’s UAE citizenship only after they filed the original disclosure.
As my motion explains, if that is true, then either World Liberty’s lawyers failed to conduct appropriate diligence, or World Liberty did not give its lawyers a straight answer. When we asked how this happened, World Liberty refused to tell us.
Token holders deserve to know whether the projects they invest in are telling the truth, both to the public and to courts. I am filing this motion to hold World Liberty and its lawyers accountable for what I believe was a misleading disclosure to the Court, and to make sure that the cost of World Liberty’s gamesmanship falls on them, not on me.
And after my sanctions motion is resolved in federal court, I will re-file my lawsuit against World Liberty in California state court.
I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves.

[AnthropicAI]New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.
Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so.
These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.
For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa
Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06
We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).

Image the world in 50 years. 1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices. 2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize. 3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc. 4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record. 5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful. 6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. item.title: [AnthropicAI]We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life. Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown. With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery. Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells. For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science. In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them. Read more:
